opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's become one of the tools I lean on most day to day. Before a meeting, whether it's a customer, a potential partner, or someone from government, I can just ask it to put together a briefing. It goes off and pulls from our internal systems: past email threads, notes from previous meetings, what's in the CRM, any relevant docs our team has written. It combines that with what's out there publicly about the company or the person, then comes back with a really coherent picture of who I'm meeting, what we've discussed before, where things stand, and what they're likely to care about.

What makes it useful versus just a search tool is the synthesis. It isn't handing me fifty links to read; it's doing the reasoning and producing something I can absorb in five minutes walking into the room. And because it's grounded in our own data, it catches the stuff I'd otherwise miss, like a follow-up someone on the team promised three months ago, or a concern the customer raised with a different person at Cohere that never made it to me.

Honestly, that's the whole thesis behind North. The value isn't the model in isolation, it's the model plugged securely into all the context an organization actually has. When you see it save you an hour of prep before every meeting, and multiply that across an entire company, that's where the real productivity gains show up.

r001.rationale: The response says the tool draws on internal past email threads and meeting notes, alongside public information, to prepare a briefing.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing I keep coming back to is that it just saves me the hour I used to spend cobbling context together before a call. If I'm about to meet with, say, a bank or a telco, I'd normally be bouncing between their latest earnings, some news coverage, our own CRM notes, Slack threads from the account team, and whatever I half-remember from the last conversation. North's deep research tool goes and does that for me. It pulls from the public web, but it also pulls from our internal systems, so I get one briefing that says: here's what this company is doing, here's what we've actually talked to them about, here's what's changed since the last time we spoke, and here are the open questions.

That second part, the internal data, is really what makes it useful rather than just a nicer search. A generic model can tell me what a company announced last quarter. It can't tell me that two of our engineers had a technical call with them three weeks ago and that there was a concern about deployment in their private cloud. That's the stuff that actually changes how I walk into the room.

The other thing I'd say is that it's good at being honest about what it doesn't know. It'll cite where something came from, and if the internal record is thin, it says so. For meeting prep that matters, because the worst outcome is walking in confidently wrong. I'd rather it tell me "we don't have much on this" so I can go ask a human.

And frankly, I'm dogfooding. If I'm going to tell enterprises that this is how work should feel, I should be living it. The places where it frustrates me are usually the places we end up fixing next.

r001.rationale: The response credits the tool with combining public information and internal sources such as CRM notes and account-team Slack threads, but does not clearly say it accesses Gomez’s personal communication history.

astra-6.text: For meeting prep, the useful thing is pulling together context that’s scattered across the company. You want to know: What have we discussed with this customer? What did we commit to? What’s still unresolved? Instead of hunting through documents and conversations, I can ask for a briefing and then dig into the underlying sources. That means I can spend my time thinking about the meeting—what questions to ask and what decisions we need to make.
